title: Sumitra's blessing
hookLine: bark clothes are brought out, Sita doesn't know how to put them on, and Lakshmana's mother gives him one verse
tomorrow: why does Rama slip away before dawn?

cards: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana walk to the palace on foot. Crowds line the streets, and Valmiki lets us hear them: people who cheered for the coronation this morning are weeping now, and some openly criticize the king.
Inside, the whole family is waiting: the old king, the queens, counselors, priests. This is the last room before the road. And someone has brought a pile of clothes made of tree bark.

teach.b: Dasharatha begs Rama, one last time, to stay just one night. Rama gently refuses. The king orders the army and the treasury to go with him, and Rama turns it down.
Why keep the rope, he asks, once you've given away the elephant? Then Kaikeyi hands out the bark garments. Rama and Lakshmana trade their fine clothes for them.
Sita stands holding hers, confused. She has never worn anything like it. She tries, can't, and starts to cry.
Rama ties it for her, over her silk. Vasishtha, watching, finally loses his temper with Kaikeyi.

teach.h: VASISHTHA: SITA WASN'T IN THE BOONS.
teach.b: Sita was never part of the boons, he says. Then the mothers speak. And Sumitra gives her son Lakshmana one verse: rāmaṃ daśarathaṃ viddhi māṃ viddhi janakātmajām, ayodhyām aṭavīṃ viddhi, gaccha tāta yathāsukham.
Think of Rama as your father Dasharatha. Think of Sita as me, your mother.
Think of the forest as Ayodhya. Go, my son, and go happily. A mother sends her son into exile by telling him he isn't leaving home at all.
Centuries later, Tulsidas, retelling the Ramayana in Hindi, gives Sumitra a line in the same spirit: Ayodhya is wherever Rama lives.
For devotees, that's the teaching under the verse. Home isn't a city. It's being near God and the people you love.
It's why a family that moves across an ocean can carry its little home shrine with it, and still be home.

how: Sumitra's verse, rāmaṃ daśarathaṃ viddhi, is taught as a picture of how love makes any place home; Tulsidas's Hindi Ramcharitmanas gives her a line in the same spirit: Ayodhya is wherever Rama lives.

o: Bharata's journey home to claim the crown
the king's last order sending the army after Rama
the exiles' leaving, with bark clothes and farewells

p: think of the forest as Ayodhya
Sita was never part of the boons
why keep one once the other's gone

s: Sita knows at once how to wear bark clothes
she can't tie it, and Rama ties it for her.
Sumitra tells Lakshmana to think of Sita as his mother
and Rama as his father, and the forest as Ayodhya.
Vasishtha says Sita must wear bark like the brothers
he says the opposite: Sita was never part of the boons.

games.q: you're Rama. the king offers the army and the treasury to go with you into exile. what do you say?
o: take them; the forest is dangerous.
why keep the rope once you've given away the elephant?
games.why: he has given up the kingdom; keeping its army would be keeping the rope. he goes as an exile, fully.

practice: Try Sumitra's words on wherever you are. If you pray, picture the face of God you know best, here in this room with you; if you don't, picture the people you love.
On a breath in, notice this room, this chair, this light; on a breath out, let it be home. If your mind drifts somewhere you'd rather be, gently bring it back, and call this Ayodhya.

wordCard.voice: The departure, part two: the goodbyes. Bark clothes, Rama tying Sita's, and Sumitra's verse: think of the forest as Ayodhya.

orig.note: Sanskrit valkala: bark, and clothing made of bark, worn by forest ascetics.

carryVoice: Hold on to it: Ayodhya is wherever Rama is. Next week, the road. Day five hundred thirty-two, done.
